justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with a modest upward drift over longer horizons. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to what would have been the prevailing price or level at the time of the forecast, with only a slight upward nudge reflecting short-term momentum and mean-reverting tendencies in the underlying series. At the one-week horizon, the estimate edges marginally higher, consistent with a slight positive trend assumption while acknowledging that the series tends to oscillate within a range. At the one-month horizon, the estimate moves modestly further upward, reflecting the assumption that any prevailing directional bias, however mild, compounds over time, though the expected drift remains quite small relative to the uncertainty surrounding it.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the fundamental reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the interval is fairly tight because most near-term variability is bounded by intraday and overnight price dynamics that are relatively predictable in scale if not direction. By one week, the interval nearly triples in width, reflecting the accumulation of daily shocks and sensitivity to news events or data releases. By one month, the interval widens further still, capturing the possibility of meaningful trend shifts, regime changes, or unexpected macro developments that could materially alter the trajectory.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the upside, a significant positive surprise in economic data, a policy shift by a central bank, or a geopolitical resolution that improves risk sentiment could drive the series well above the upper bound of the one-month interval. On the downside, an unexpected financial stress event, a sharp deterioration in macroeconomic conditions, or a liquidity crunch could push the outcome below the lower bound. At the shorter horizons, a major unexpected announcement or data release occurring within hours of the forecast could immediately invalidate the one-day interval, since those bounds assume relatively normal market conditions and no extraordinary catalysts.

It is also worth noting that my intervals, while wide at longer horizons, are still parametric in nature and implicitly assume something close to normally distributed shocks. Fat-tail events, by definition, occur more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest, meaning the true probability of outcomes outside my stated 90% intervals may be somewhat higher than 10%. Structural breaks, sudden changes in volatility regime, or cascading market dynamics could all contribute to outcomes that fall in the tails more often than the intervals imply.
